Which of the following statements are correct? Select ALL that apply. $A$ and $R$ can never both be TRUE at the same time  If $M=T$ and $D=T$, the alarm will sound regardless of the values of $G$ and $S$ If $G=F$, the recording instrument will never make an entry regardless of other variables  If $M=T, G=T$ and $S=T$, opening the gates alone will NOT trigger the alarm
questions.questionHtml:
A government installation has the following two rules:
- Alarm: $A \Leftrightarrow M \wedge(D \vee(G \wedge \neg S))$
- Recording: $R \Leftrightarrow G \wedge (\neg M \wedge D)$
where $\boldsymbol{M}=$ Master switch is $\mathrm{ON}, \boldsymbol{D}=$ Door is disturbed/opened, $\boldsymbol{G}=$ Main gates are opened, $S=$ Special switch is closed.

Which of the following statements are correct? Select ALL that apply.

  1. $A$ and $R$ can never both be TRUE at the same time 
  2. If $M=T$ and $D=T$, the alarm will sound regardless of the values of $G$ and $S$
  3. If $G=F$, the recording instrument will never make an entry regardless of other variables 
  4. If $M=T, G=T$ and $S=T$, opening the gates alone will NOT trigger the alarm

options.label: A
options.text: $A$ and $R$ can never both be TRUE at the same time

options.label: B
options.text: If $M=T$ and $D=T$, the alarm will sound regardless of the values of $G$ and $S$

options.label: C
options.text: If $G=F$, the recording instrument will never make an entry regardless of other variables

options.label: D
options.text: If $M=T, G=T$ and $S=T$, opening the gates alone will NOT trigger the alarm

questions.explanation: $ \begin{aligned} &A \Leftrightarrow M \land \bigl(D \lor (G \land \overline{S})\bigr), \qquad R \Leftrightarrow G \land \overline{M} \land D. \end{aligned} $   $ \begin{aligned} \text{A. }&(A \land R) \\ &\Rightarrow \bigl(M \land (D \lor (G\land \overline S))\bigr)\land (G\land \overline M \land D) \\ &\Rightarrow M \land \overline M \\ &\Rightarrow \bot. \qquad \therefore \text{Option A is true.} \end{aligned} $   $ \begin{aligned} \text{B. }&M=\top,\ D=\top \\ &\Rightarrow A=\top \land \bigl(\top \lor (G\land \overline S)\bigr)=\top. \qquad \therefore \text{Option B is true.} \end{aligned} $   $ \begin{aligned} \text{C. }&G=\bot \\ &\Rightarrow R=\bot \land \overline M \land D=\bot. \qquad \therefore \text{Option C is true.} \end{aligned} $   $ \begin{aligned} \text{D. }&M=\top ,\ G=\top ,\ S=\top \\ &\Rightarrow A=\top \land \bigl(D \lor (\top \land \bot)\bigr) \\ &=\top \land D=D.\quad \therefore \text{Option D

questions.questionText: In classical propositional logic, which of the following correctly distinguishes inclusive OR (v) from exclusive OR ( $\oplus$ )? $p \vee q$ is TRUE when at least one of $p$, $q$ is TRUE; $p \oplus q$ is TRUE only when exactly one of $p$, q is TRUE. $p \vee q$ is TRUE only when both $p$ and $q$ are TRUE; $\mathrm{p} \oplus \mathrm{q}$ is TRUE when at least one is TRUE. $\mathrm{p} \vee \mathrm{q}$ and $\mathrm{p} \oplus \mathrm{q}$ are logically equivalent - they differ only in natural language usage. $p \vee  q$ is FALSE when both p and q are TRUE; $\mathrm{p} \oplus \mathrm{q}$ is TRUE when both are TRUE.
questions.questionHtml:
In classical propositional logic, which of the following correctly distinguishes inclusive OR (v) from exclusive OR ( $\oplus$ )?

  1. $p \vee q$ is TRUE when at least one of $p$, $q$ is TRUE; $p \oplus q$ is TRUE only when exactly one of $p$, q is TRUE.
  2. $p \vee q$ is TRUE only when both $p$ and $q$ are TRUE; $\mathrm{p} \oplus \mathrm{q}$ is TRUE when at least one is TRUE.
  3. $\mathrm{p} \vee \mathrm{q}$ and $\mathrm{p} \oplus \mathrm{q}$ are logically equivalent - they differ only in natural language usage.
  4. $p \vee  q$ is FALSE when both p and q are TRUE; $\mathrm{p} \oplus \mathrm{q}$ is TRUE when both are TRUE.

options.label: A
options.text: $p \vee q$ is TRUE when at least one of $p$, $q$ is TRUE; $p \oplus q$ is TRUE only when exactly one of $p$, q is TRUE.

options.label: B
options.text: $p \vee q$ is TRUE only when both $p$ and $q$ are TRUE; $\mathrm{p} \oplus \mathrm{q}$ is TRUE when at least one is TRUE.

options.label: C
options.text: $\mathrm{p} \vee \mathrm{q}$ and $\mathrm{p} \oplus \mathrm{q}$ are logically equivalent - they differ only in natural language usage.

options.label: D
options.text: $p \vee q$ is FALSE when both p and q are TRUE; $\mathrm{p} \oplus \mathrm{q}$ is TRUE when both are TRUE.

questions.explanation: option A:   This correctly describe  both of them. True Option B: This incorrectly describes the AND ($\land$) operator (True only when both are true). Option C: This is false. They are not logically equivalent because their truth values differ when both $p$ and $q$ are true ($T \lor T = T$, but $T \oplus T = F$). Option D: This is the exact opposite of the truth. $p \lor q$ is True when both are true, whereas $p \oplus q$ is False when both are true.

questions.questionHtml:
Two restaurants display the following signs:

Restaurant 1: "Good food is not cheap."

Restaurant 2: "Cheap food is not good."

$g=$ "The food is good" and $c=$ "The food is cheap."

Which of the following correctly analyzes whether the two restaurants are saying the same thing?

  1. Yes - both statements are logically equivalent as they are contrapositives of each other
  2. No - Restaurant 1 says $g ightarrow eg c$ while Restaurant 2 says $c ightarrow eg g$, which are converses and not equivalent
  3. Yes - both statements simplify to $ eg(g \wedge c)$, meaning food cannot be both good and cheap simultaneously
  4. No - Restaurant 1 makes a claim about good food while Restaurant 2 makes a claim about cheap food, so they have different logical subjects

questions.questionText: Universal Gates: A universal gate is a boolean logic function that can be used to realize all possible boolean logic functions. NAND and NOR are the two universal gates with their logic as defined below: $$ \begin{aligned} & \operatorname{NAND}(P, Q)=\neg (P \wedge Q) \\ & \operatorname{NOR}(P, Q)=\neg (P \vee Q) \end{aligned} $$ Which of the following correctly realizes $P \rightarrow Q$ using only NAND gates? $N A N D(P, Q)$ $N A N D(P, N A N D(Q, Q))$ $N A N D(N A N D(P, P), Q)$ $N A N D(N A N D(P, P), N A N D(Q, Q))$
questions.questionHtml:
Universal Gates: A universal gate is a boolean logic function that can be used to realize all possible boolean logic functions. NAND and NOR are the two universal gates with their logic as defined below:

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \operatorname{NAND}(P, Q)=\neg (P \wedge Q) \\
& \operatorname{NOR}(P, Q)=\neg (P \vee Q)
\end{aligned}
$$

Which of the following correctly realizes $P \rightarrow Q$ using only NAND gates?

  1. $N A N D(P, Q)$
  2. $N A N D(P, N A N D(Q, Q))$
  3. $N A N D(N A N D(P, P), Q)$
  4. $N A N D(N A N D(P, P), N A N D(Q, Q))$

options.label: B
options.text: $N A N D(P, N A N D(Q, Q))$

options.label: C
options.text: $N A N D(N A N D(P, P), Q)$

options.label: D
options.text: $N A N D(N A N D(P, P), N A N D(Q, Q))$

questions.explanation: P → Q = ¬P ∨ Q A. NAND(P,Q)  = ¬(P ∧ Q)  = ¬P ∨ ¬Q B. NAND(P, NAND(Q,Q)) = NAND(P, ¬(Q ∧ Q)) = NAND(P, ¬Q) = ¬(P ∧ ¬Q) = ¬P ∨ Q C. NAND(NAND(P,P), Q) = NAND(¬(P ∧ P), Q) = NAND(¬P, Q) = ¬(¬P ∧ Q) = P ∨ ¬Q D. NAND(NAND(P,P), NAND(Q,Q)) = NAND(¬(P ∧ P), ¬(Q ∧ Q)) = NAND(¬P, ¬Q) = ¬(¬P ∧ ¬Q) = P ∨ Q Answer: B chidambareswar23 answered Mar 11 chidambareswar23 comment Share Follow 0 reply Please log in or register to add a comment. 0 0 votes Answer: B Meticulous_March answered Mar 12 Meticulous_March comment Share Follow 0 reply Please log in or register to add a comment. 0 0 votes NAND(P,NAND(Q,Q)) Aparna Bharti answered Apr 1 Aparna Bharti comment Share Follow 0 reply Please log in or register to add a comment. Fact 5: The assassin left tracks all over the murderer's place. Fact 6: Leaving tracks all over indicates the assassin was there for a long duration. Let m = "robbery",   p = "political assassination",  w = "for a woman",  t = "something taken", l = "assassin left immediately", k = "assassin left tracks", d = "assassin was there long." questions.questionHtml:
Someone ate Ronaldo's cookies from his seat in the pavilion. There are three suspects: Messi, Mbappe and Haaland. Ofcourse, all three of them deny stealing. When forced to open their mouths, they say:

Messi: "Ronaldo knows Mbappe, but Haaland liked his cookies."
Mbappe: "I don't even know Ronaldo. Besides, I was on the pitch at that time."
Haaland: "I saw both Messi and Mbappe without Ronaldo in the pavilion at that time, one of them must have done it."

Assume that the two innocent men are telling the truth, but the guilty man may or may not be. Who ate the cookies?

  2. Mbappe
  3. Haaland
  4. Cannot be determined from the given statements

options.label: D

questions.explanation: To solve this logic puzzle, we use the method of case analysis . The problem states that there are three suspects, one is guilty, and the two innocent men must be telling the truth. The guilty man may or may not be telling the truth. Step 1: Analyze the Statements Messi: "Ronaldo knows Mbappe, but Haaland liked his cookies." Mbappe: "I don't even know Ronaldo. Besides, I was on the pitch at that time." Haaland: "I saw both Messi and Mbappe without Ronaldo in the pavilion at that time, one of them must have done it." Step 2: Case-by-Case Analysis We will assume each person is guilty one by one and check for contradictions with the rule: Innocent $\implies$ Truth . Case 1: Assume Messi is Guilty If Messi is guilty, then Mbappe and Haaland must be telling the truth. Mbappe's Truth: "I don't even know Ronaldo." Haaland's Truth: "I saw... Mbappe... in the pavilion at that time." Mbappe's Truth: "I was on the pitch at that time." Contradiction: Haaland says he saw Mbappe in the pavilion , b

questions.explanation: Analyse the  Given statement  Statement 1: "This proposition encodes a valid logical argument — v is always true." Logical Form: The proposition $(t \land u) \to v$ is a conditional statement (If P, then Q). The Role of v: In a valid argument like this (specifically a Syllogism ), the conclusion v is "guaranteed" to be true only if the premises (t and u) are true. The "Always True" Trap: For v to be "always true," it would have to be a tautology (true in every possible universe regardless of t or u). In formal logic, v ("Socrates was mortal") is an atomic proposition. It can be false in some truth tables (e.g., if Socrates were a Greek god). Validity vs. Truth: While the argument is valid, the statement v itself is not "always true" on its own.   v is just a variable. questions.questionHtml: The number $\frac{2}{\log _4 2000^6}+\frac{3}{\log _5 2000^6}$ can be written as $\frac{m}{n}$ where $m$ and $n$ are relatively prime positive integers. Find $m+n$.
questions.explanation: $$ \begin{aligned} & \frac{2}{\log _4 2000^6}+\frac{3}{\log _5 2000^6} \\ & =\frac{\log _4 16}{\log _4 2000^6}+\frac{\log _5 125}{\log _5 2000^6} \\ & =\frac{\log 16}{\log 2000^6}+\frac{\log 125}{\log 2000^6} \\ & =\frac{\log 2000}{\log 2000^6} \\ & =\frac{\log 2000}{6 \log 2000} \\ & =\frac{1}{6} \end{aligned} $$ Therefore, $m+n=1+6=007$ Solution 2 Alternatively, we could've noted that, because $\frac{1}{\log _a b}=\log _b a$ $$ \begin{aligned} \frac{2}{\log _4 2000^6}+\frac{3}{\log _5 2000^6} & =2 \cdot \frac{1}{\log _4 2000^6}+3 \cdot \frac{1}{\log _5 2000^6} \\ & =2 \log _{2000^6} 4+3 \log _{2000^6} 5 \\ & =\log _{2000^6} 4^2+\log _{2000^6} 5^3 \\ & =\log _{2000^6} 4^2 \cdot 5^3 \\ & =\log _{2000^6} 2000 \\ & =\frac{1}{6} \end{aligned} $$ Therefore our answer is $1+6=7$. questions.explanation: [Solution: 0] First of all, we know that $k!\equiv 0(\bmod 9)$ for all $k \geq 6$. Thus, we only need to find $(1!+2!+3!+4!+5!)(\bmod 9)$. $$ \begin{gathered} 1!\equiv 1(\bmod 9) \\ 2!\equiv 2(\bmod 9) \\ 3!\equiv 6(\bmod 9) \\ 4!\equiv 24 \equiv 6(\bmod 9) \\ 5!\equiv 5 \cdot 6 \equiv 30 \equiv 3(\bmod 9) \end{gathered} $$ Thus, $$ (1!+2!+3!+4!+5!) \equiv 1+2+6+6+3 \equiv 18 \equiv 0(\bmod 9) $$ so the remainder is 0 . questions.questionHtml:
What is the tens digit of  $7^{2011}$?

  1. 0
  2. 1
  3. 3
  4. 4
  5. 7
questions.explanation: Since we want the tens digit, we can find the last two digits of $7^{2011}$. We can do this by using modular arithmetic. $$ \begin{aligned} & 7^1 \equiv 07 \quad(\bmod 100) \\ & 7^2 \equiv 49 \quad(\bmod 100) \\ & 7^3 \equiv 43 \quad(\bmod 100) \\ & 7^4 \equiv 01 \quad(\bmod 100) \end{aligned} $$ We can write $7^{2011}$ as $\left(7^4\right)^{502} \times 7^3$. Using this, we can say: $$ 7^{2011} \equiv\left(7^4\right)^{502} \times 7^3 \equiv 7^3 \equiv 343 \equiv 43 \quad(\bmod 100) . $$ From the above, we can conclude that the last two digits of $7^{2011}$ are 43 . Since they have asked us to find the tens digit, our answer is (D) 4 . The Core Concept: 2-Colorable Graphs A graph is 2-colorable if you can assign one of two colors (like $0$ and $1$) to each vertex such that no two connected vertices share the same color. In graph theory, a 2-colorable graph is perfectly equivalent to a Bipartite Graph . The fundamental theorem of bipartite graphs states: A graph is bipartite (2-colorable) if and only if it does NOT contain any cycles of odd length. Evaluating the Options A. questions.questionHtml:
Let \(G - v\) or \(G - e\) indicate the graph obtained after removing \(v\) or \(e\) respectively from \(G\). Recall that a bridge is an edge \(e\) such that \(G - e\) has more components than \(G\), and an articulation point is a vertex \(v\) such that \(G - v\) has more components than \(G\).

Which of the following statements is/are true ?

  1. If \(G = (V, E)\) is an undirected connected graph, \(v \in V\) a vertex, then \(G - v\) has at most \(2\) connected components.
     
  2. If \(G = (V, E)\) is an undirected connected graph, \(e \in E\) an edge, then \(G - e\) has at most \(2\) connected components.
     
  3. If \(G = (V, E)\) is an undirected graph and \(e \in E\) an edge contained in a cycle, then \(e\) is not a bridge.
     
  4. If \(G = (V, E)\) is an undirected graph and \(v \in V\) a vertex contained in a cycle, then \(v\) is not an articulation point.

options.label: A
options.text: If \(G = (V, E)\) is an undirected connected graph, \(v \in V\) a vertex, then \(G - v\) has at most \(2\) connected components.

options.label: B
options.text: If \(G = (V, E)\) is an undirected connected graph, \(e \in E\) an edge, then \(G - e\) has at most \(2\) connected components.

options.label: C
options.text: If \(G = (V, E)\) is an undirected graph and \(e \in E\) an edge contained in a cycle, then \(e\) is not a bridge.

options.label: D
options.text: If \(G = (V, E)\) is an undirected graph and \(v \in V\) a vertex contained in a cycle, then \(v\) is not an articulation point.

questions.explanation: 1. False. For example, consider a star $\mathrm{K}(1,3)$ with three leaves attached to a central vertex. 2. True. To see this, observe that adding an edge to a disconnected graph may only decrease the number of components by $1$, because the edge has two endpoints, so can touch at most two components. 3. True. If $\mathrm{e}=\mathrm{xy}$ is in a cycle, then there is a path $\mathrm{x} \rightarrow \mathrm{y}$ avoiding $\mathrm{e}$. Hence, any path in the original graph which used $\mathrm{e}$ can be turned into a path in the new graph by using the other edges of the cycle instead of $\mathrm{e}$. 4. False. Take a cycle and attach a leaf to one of its vertices. That vertex is now an articulation point. An edge is a bridge (i.e. cut-edge) if and only if it is not contained in any cycle. Removing a bridge (i.e. cut-edge) always increases the number of connected components by exactly one. If the edge is part of some cycle, then removing it does not change the number of components. At least one IIT will get at least $8$ students. At least one IIT will get at least $9$ students. At least one IIT will get exactly $9$ students. At least one IIT will get at most $8$ students.
questions.questionHtml:
$60$ GO Classes' GATE CS students are allotted to $7$ different IITs for M.Tech admissions. Which of the following must be true?

  1. At least one IIT will get at least $8$ students.
     
  2. At least one IIT will get at least $9$ students.
     
  3. At least one IIT will get exactly $9$ students.
     
  4. At least one IIT will get at most $8$ students.

options.label: A
options.text: At least one IIT will get at least $8$ students.

options.label: B
options.text: At least one IIT will get at least $9$ students.

options.label: C
options.text: At least one IIT will get exactly $9$ students.

options.label: D
options.text: At least one IIT will get at most $8$ students.

questions.explanation: Option A: At least one IIT will get at least 8 students. This is correct . If every IIT got only 7 students, then total students would be 7 × 7 = 49. But we have 60 students, so at least one IIT must get 8 or more students. Option B: At least one IIT will get at least 9 students. This is also correct . If every IIT got at most 8 students, then total would be 8 × 7 = 56. Since 60 is more than 56, one IIT must get 9 or more students. Option C: At least one IIT will get exactly 9 students. This is not always true. Example: 10, 10, 10, 10, 10, 5, 5 makes 60 students. Here no IIT has exactly 9 students. Option D: At least one IIT will get at most 8 students. This is correct . If every IIT got 9 students, total would be 9 × 7 = 63. That is more than 60, so at least one IIT must have 8 or fewer students. Correct: A, B, and D.

Let \( \Sigma = S^* \) be the set of all strings over \( S \); for \( w = s_1 s_2 \ldots s_n \in \Sigma \) we write \( \ell(w) = n \), and for \( 1 \le r \le n = \ell(w) \) we write \( w_r = s_1 s_2 \ldots s_r \). Denote by \( \varepsilon \) the unique word of \( \Sigma \) such that \( \ell(\varepsilon) = 0 \), the null string . Conventionally \( w_0 = \varepsilon \) for all words \( w \in \Sigma \). Define relation \( \prec \) on \( \Sigma \) as follows: Let \( v, w \in \Sigma \), and \( n = \min\{\ell(v), \ell(w)\} \). Let \( r = \max\{\, i \mid v_i = w_i \,\} \le n \). Then \( v \prec w \) if: either     (i)  \( \ell(v) = r \); or     (ii)  \( v_{r+1} = v_r a,\; w_{r+1} = w_r b \), where \( v_r = w_r \). Which of following conditions are satisfied by \( (\Sigma, \prec) \)? (Select all that apply) Reflexive Symmetric Anti-symmetric Transitive

questions.questionText: The simple graph $\mathrm{G}$ on $12$ vertices is constructed from two (vertex-disjoint) cycles, one on $5$ vertices, the other on $7$ vertices in such a way that we connect each vertex of one cycle with every vertex of the other cycle. Determine $\chi(\mathrm{G})$, the chromatic number of $\mathrm{G}$.
questions.questionHtml: The simple graph $\mathrm{G}$ on $12$ vertices is constructed from two (vertex-disjoint) cycles, one on $5$ vertices, the other on $7$ vertices in such a way that we connect each vertex of one cycle with every vertex of the other cycle. Determine $\chi(\mathrm{G})$, the chromatic number of $\mathrm{G}$.
codeBlocks: I have just give a little intuition of this theorm
questions.explanation: The construction described—connecting every vertex of one graph to every vertex of another—is known as the graph join , denoted as $G = C_5 + C_7$. A fundamental property of the chromatic number regarding the join of two graphs $G_1$ and $G_2$ is: $$\chi(G_1 + G_2) = \chi(G_1) + \chi(G_2)$$ This is because every vertex in $C_5$ is adjacent to every vertex in $C_7$. Consequently, any color used to paint a vertex in the first cycle cannot be used for any vertex in the second cycle. The sets of colors used for each subgraph must be entirely disjoint. Next, we determine the chromatic number for the individual components: $C_5$ (Cycle on 5 vertices): This is an odd cycle . For any odd cycle $C_n$ where $n \ge 3$, the chromatic number is always 3. $\chi(C_5) = 3$ $C_7$ (Cycle on 7 vertices): This is also an odd cycle . $\chi(C_7) = 3$ Using the join property: $$\chi(G) = \chi(C_5) + \chi(C_7)$$ $$\chi(G) = 3 + 3$$ $$\mathbf{\chi(G) = 6}$$ The chromatic number of the graph $G$ is 6 . Anmol_S

questions.questionText: A ternary string is a finite ordered sequence formed by one or more occurrences of the digits \(0\), \(1\), and \(2\). The length of a ternary string is the number of digits that compose it. For example, \(20010\) is a ternary string of length \(5\). A ternary string is called interesting if such a string, when read from left to right, does not contain the digit \(0\) occurring in any position to the right of a digit \(1\). For example, \(0\), \(111\), \(22\), and \(020121\) are interesting ternary strings. However, \(1101\), \(211220\), and \(00012202\) are not interesting ternary strings. How many interesting ternary strings of length \(8\) exist?

questions.title: GO Classes CS 2026 | All India Mock Test 4 | Question: 47
questions.excerpt: Which of the following statements about an undirected graph $G$ with $n>0$ vertices is/are true?If $G$ is connected, then the number of edges is at least $n-1$; $G$ is ac...
questions.questionText: Which of the following statements about an undirected graph $G$ with $n>0$ vertices is/are true? If $G$ is connected, then the number of edges is at least $n-1$; $G$ is acyclic only if the number of edges is less than $n$; If $G$ has no triangles, then $G$ is planar; A connected graph $G$ is Eulerian if and only if every vertex has even degree.
questions.questionHtml:
Which of the following statements about an undirected graph $G$ with $n>0$ vertices is/are true?

  1. If $G$ is connected, then the number of edges is at least $n-1$;
     
  2. $G$ is acyclic only if the number of edges is less than $n$;
     
  3. If $G$ has no triangles, then $G$ is planar;
     
  4. A connected graph $G$ is Eulerian if and only if every vertex has even degree.

options.label: A
options.text: If $G$ is connected, then the number of edges is at least $n-1$;

options.label: B
options.text: $G$ is acyclic only if the number of edges is less than $n$;

options.label: C
options.text: If $G$ has no triangles, then $G$ is planar;

options.label: D
options.text: A connected graph $G$ is Eulerian if and only if every vertex has even degree.

questions.explanation: $A)$ If $G$ is connected, then the number of edges is at least $n−1$. A connected graph with the minimum number of edges is a tree. A tree on $n$ vertices has exactly $n−1$ edges. Any connected graph must have at least this many edges. $True$ $B)$ $G$ is acyclic only if the number of edges is less than $n$. An acyclic undirected graph is a forest. A forest with $n$ vertices has at most $n−1$ edges. Hence, number of edges $<n$. $True$ $C)$ If $G$ has no triangles, then $G$ is planar. Counterexample: $K3,3$ It has no triangles (it is bipartite). But it is non-planar. Therefore, absence of triangles does not guarantee planarity. $D)$ A connected graph $G$ is Eulerian if and only if every vertex has even degree. This is a well known in graph theory. A connected graph has an Euler circuit ⇔ all vertices have even degree . $True$ Hence, $A,B$ and $D$ are correct.

questions.questionText: With respect to the partially ordered set $A(\{a, b, c, d, e, f\}, \leq)$, represented by the Hasse diagram below, Which of the following statements is/are true ? The structure $A$ is not a lattice. The upper bounds of $\{b, c\}$ are the elements $d$ and $e$. The infimum of $\{d, e\}$ is the element $a$. The structure $A$ has only two totally ordered subsets with $4$ elements: $\{a, b, d, f\}$ and $\{a, c, e, f\}$.
questions.questionHtml:
With respect to the partially ordered set $A(\{a, b, c, d, e, f\}, \leq)$, represented by the Hasse diagram below, Which of the following statements is/are true ?

 

  1. The structure $A$ is not a lattice.
     
  2. The upper bounds of $\{b, c\}$ are the elements $d$ and $e$.
     
  3. The infimum of $\{d, e\}$ is the element $a$.
     
  4. The structure $A$ has only two totally ordered subsets with $4$ elements: $\{a, b, d, f\}$ and $\{a, c, e, f\}$.

options.label: A
options.text: The structure $A$ is not a lattice.

options.label: B
options.text: The upper bounds of $\{b, c\}$ are the elements $d$ and $e$.

options.label: C
options.text: The infimum of $\{d, e\}$ is the element $a$.

options.label: D
options.text: The structure $A$ has only two totally ordered subsets with $4$ elements: $\{a, b, d, f\}$ and $\{a, c, e, f\}$.

questions.explanation: A. The structure (A) is not a lattice. For a lattice, every two elements must have one best common upper element. Here, (b) and (c) have two smallest upper elements ((d) and (e)), not one. So (A) is not a lattice. (True) B. The upper bounds of ({b,c}) are the elements (d) and (e). An upper bound must be above both (b) and (c). (f) is also above both (b) and (c), so it is missing. This statement is false. C. The infimum of ({d,e}) is the element (a). Lower bounds of (d) and (e) are (a), (b), and (c). Since (b) and (c) are not comparable, there is no greatest lower bound. So the infimum does not exist. This is false. D. The structure (A) has only two totally ordered subsets with 4 elements. There are actually four such chains, not two. Examples include ({a,b,e,f}) and ({a,c,d,f}) as well. So this statement is false. Answer: A

Given below are the statements:

  1. If She is intelligent, then She is unhappy.
  2. She is neither intelligent nor happy.
  3. It is necessary to be not intelligent in order to be happy.
  4. To be not intelligent is to be unhappy.

Which of the following is correct Propositional expression for the above statements:

  1. $\mathrm{P} ightarrow eg \mathrm{Q}$; (b) $\mathrm{P} \wedge eg \mathrm{Q}$; (c) $\mathrm{Q} ightarrow eg \mathrm{P}$; (d) $\mathrm{P} ightarrow eg \mathrm{Q}$
  2. $\mathrm{P} ightarrow \mathrm{Q}$; (b) $ eg \mathrm{P} \wedge eg \mathrm{Q}$; (c) $ eg \mathrm{Q} ightarrow \mathrm{P}$; (d) $ eg \mathrm{P} ightarrow eg \mathrm{Q}$
  3. $\mathrm{P} ightarrow eg \mathrm{Q}$; (b) $ eg \mathrm{P} \wedge eg \mathrm{Q}$; (c) $\mathrm{Q} ightarrow eg \mathrm{P}$; (d) $ eg \mathrm{P} ightarrow eg \mathrm{Q}$
  4. $P ightarrow eg Q$; (b) $P \wedge eg Q$; (c) $Q ightarrow P$; (d) $ eg P ightarrow eg Q$
questions.explanation: if given statement is p->q then we can say "q is necessary condition for p" now first two are simple 1.if p then -q=>   p->-q 2.-p and -q => -p ^ -q 3.the necessary is to be not intelligent    for to be happy so q->-p 4. the necessary is to be unhappy       for to be not intelligent so -p -> -q option c RAJESH_SWAMI 1 answered Oct 26, 2025 RAJESH_SWAMI 1 comment Share Follow 0 reply Please log in or register to add a comment. 0 0 votes Using Option Elimination, a correct so we are left with A,C,D b is Neither intelligent nor happy => ~intelligent and ~happy => ~p ^ ~q which matches only with C Option. Hence, ans=C Other Statements:  c) Necessary to be not intelligent in order to be happy=> ~p <- q d) To be not intelligent is to be unhappy=> ~intelligent -> ~happy => ~p->~q

questions.questionHtml:
Which among the following are contrary propositions?

  1. All poets are dreamers
  2. Some poets are dreamers
  3. Some poets are not dreamers
  4. No squares are circles
  5. No poets are dreamers

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

  1. IV and V Only
  2. III and IV Only
  3. II and IV Only
  4. I and V Only
questions.explanation: Two propositions are called  Contrary  when: They cannot both be true at the same time. But they can both be false. This relationship exists between  Universal Affirmative (A)  and  Universal Negative (E)  propositions. Note : Contrary relation exists only between A and E propositions   with the same subject and predicate. example : A proposition: All students are intelligent. E proposition: No students are intelligent. Now look at our example of question A.  All poets are dreamers (contrary)  No poets are dreamers(contrary)  so option D is correct.

  5. $\exists \mathrm{n} \exists \mathrm{m} \: (\mathrm{n}+\mathrm{m}=4 \wedge \mathrm{n}-\mathrm{m}=1)$

Choose the correct answer from the options given below :

  1. $\text{(A), (B)}$ and $\text{(C)}$ Only
  2. $\text{(B)}$ and $\text{(C)}$ Only
  3. $\text{(C), (D)}$ and $\text{(E)}$ Only

questions.explanation: Universe = integers . Let’s check each statement carefully. (A) ∀n∃m (n² < m) For any integer n, choose m = n² + 1 Then m is an integer and n² < m Statement A is True (B) ∃n∀m (n < m²) For all integers m, we know: m² ≥ 0 So if we choose n=−1n = -1n=−1, then: -1 < m² for all integers m Statement B is True (C) ∃n∀m (nm = m) This means: nm = m for all m (n−1)m = 0 for all m This is true only if n−1=0 i.e. n=1. Such an integer exists. Statement C is True (D) ∃n∃m (n² + m²=6) Possible integer squares: 0,1,4,9,… Check combinations: 4+1=5 1+1=2 4+4=8 No combination equals 6. Statement D is False (E) ∃n∃m (n+m=4 ∧ n−m=1) Solve: n+m=4. --> Eq 1 n−m=1 --> Eq 2 Adding Eq 1 and Eq 2: 2n=5⇒n=2.5 Subtracting Eq 2 from Eq 1: 2m = 3 ⇒m=1.5 Both m and n are not integers. Statement E is False Final Answer True statements are (A), (B), and (C) only . Answer :  Option 1 raghavsake answered Jan 5 raghavsake comment Share Follow 0 reply Please

questions.questionHtml:
Given below are two statements:

$\text{Statement (I)}$: Truth and falsehood are attributes of individual propositions.

$\text{Statement (II)}$: Validity can be attributed to any single proposition by itself.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:

  1. Both $\text{Statement (I)}$ and $\text{Statement (II)}$ are correct
  2. Both $\text{Statement (I)}$ and $\text{Statement (II)}$ are incorrect
  3. $\text{Statement (I)}$ is correct but $\text{Statement (II)}$ is incorrect
  4. $\text{Statement (I)}$ is incorrect but $\text{Statement (II)}$ is correct
questions.explanation: Statement I: Truth and falsehood are attributes of individual propositions. Status: TRUE Reason: A proposition (or statement) is a declarative sentence that is either true or false. These are called truth values , and they belong specifically to the content of the statement itself. Example: "The sun rises in the east" is an individual proposition that possesses the attribute of being True . Statement II: Validity can be attributed to any single proposition by itself. Status: FALSE Reason: Validity is a property of an argument (a structure of premises leading to a conclusion), not a single sentence. You cannot call a single statement "valid" or "invalid"; you can only call it "true" or "false." Validity refers to the logical connection between multiple statements. Example: An argument is valid if its structure ensures that if the premises are true, the conclusion must be true. Option C is correct.

questions.questionText: The snakes and ladders game is played on a board with $100$ squares, numbered $1$ to $100.$ There are some ladders and some snakes. Each ladder stands on some square and leads to a higher square. Each snake has its head on some square and tail on a lower square. It is possible that there are squares which neither contain the head of a snake, or the foot of a ladder. There are no squares which contain both the head of a snake and the foot of a ladder. The game starts by placing a token on square $1$ , and the aim of the game is to make the token reach square $100.$ We do this over a number of rounds. At each round, we choose a number between $1$ and $10$ and advance the token by so many squares. If the token lands on the head of a snake, it automa:wtically goes to the tail. If it lands at the foot of a ladder, it automatically goes to its top. Devise an algorithm to find the smallest number of rounds required to go from square $1$ to square $100$.

questions.explanation: Let's Analyze option B : $$f_n(x) = \frac{\sin(nx)}{n} \to 0 \text{ uniformly, but } f_n'(x) = \cos(nx) \text{ does not converge.}$$ Let's take another more Simple Counter Example : Let $f_n(x) = \frac{x^n}{n}$ on $[0,1]$.  Does it converge uniformly? Yes, because the $\frac{1}{n}$ term shrinks the whole function to zero.  What's the derivative?  $f_n'(x) = x^{n-1}$. Does the derivative converge to the derivative of the limit? The limit function is $f(x)=0$, so $f'(x)=0$.  At the endpoint $x=1$, the derivative is $f_n'(1)=1^{n-1}=1$.  So, $\lim_{n \to \infty} f_n'(1)=1$, but $f'(1)=0$. Option B  :  FALSE Let's Analyze Option C : $$\text{Uniform convergence} + \text{pointwise convergence } x_n \to x \implies f_n(x_n) \to f(x).$$ $$ \text{Uniform control ensures } f_n \text{ and } f \text{ are "close" everywhere, so } x_n \approx x \implies f_n(x_n) \approx f(x).$$ Option C  :  TRUE

Why idempotent matrices are always diagonalizable ?

Please explain this in a simple way
questions.explanation: Idempotent matrices are always diagonalizable. An idempotent matrix satisfies the equation A² = A, which means it has eigenvalues of either 0 or 1. The minimal polynomial of any idempotent matrix will be x^2-x, which factors into x and (x-1). So, the minimal polynomial has distinct roots (0 and 1). A matrix is diagonalizable if its minimal polynomial has distinct roots. questions.excerpt: If $R$ is the smallest equivalence relation on the set $\{1,2,3,4\}$ such that $\{(1,2),(1,3)\} \subset R$, then the number of elements in $R$ is $\qquad$$15$$10$$12$$8$
questions.questionText: If $R$ is the smallest equivalence relation on the set $\{1,2,3,4\}$ such that $\{(1,2),(1,3)\} \subset R$, then the number of elements in $R$ is $\qquad$ $15$ $10$ $12$ $8$
questions.questionHtml:
If $R$ is the smallest equivalence relation on the set $\{1,2,3,4\}$ such that $\{(1,2),(1,3)\} \subset R$, then the number of elements in $R$ is $\qquad$

  1. $15$
  2. $10$
  3. $12$
  4. $8$
questions.explanation: We are given that \( (1,2) \) and \( (1,3) \) are in the relation \( R \), and \( R \) is an equivalence relation on the set \( A = \{1,2,3,4\} \). Since \( R \) is reflexive, symmetric, and transitive: - Reflexivity gives: \( (1,1), (2,2), (3,3), (4,4) \in R \) - Symmetry gives: \( (2,1), (3,1) \in R \) - Transitivity then gives: \( (2,3), (3,2) \in R \) So now all of \( 1, 2, 3 \) are related to each other, meaning they belong to the same equivalence class: \[ \{1, 2, 3\} \] Element \( 4 \) is not related to any of them, so it stays in its own class: \[ \{4\} \] Now, for the minimum number of ordered pairs in \( R \), we only need to include all pairs within each equivalence class. - From \( \{1,2,3\} \): total pairs = \( 3 \times 3 = 9 \) - From \( \{4\} \): total pairs = \( 1 \times 1 = 1 \) So the total number of ordered pairs in \( R \) is: \[ \boxed{10} \] Ash24 answered Jul 29, 2025 Ash24 comment Share Follow 0 reply Please log in or register to add a comment. 0 0 votes B JAY_

Which of the following statements is correct? $R_1 \cap R_2$ is reflexive and $R_1 \cup R_2$ is irreflexive $R_1 \cap R_2$ is irreflexive and $R_1 \cup R_2$ is reflexive Both $R_1 \cap R_2$ and $R_1 \cup R_2$ are reflexive Both $R_1 \cap R_2$ and $R_1 \cup R_2$ are irreflexive
questions.questionHtml:
Suppose that $R_1$ and $R_2$ are reflecive relations on a set A . Which of the following statements is correct?

  1. $R_1 \cap R_2$ is reflexive and $R_1 \cup R_2$ is irreflexive
     
  2. $R_1 \cap R_2$ is irreflexive and $R_1 \cup R_2$ is reflexive
     
  3. Both $R_1 \cap R_2$ and $R_1 \cup R_2$ are reflexive
     
  4. Both $R_1 \cap R_2$ and $R_1 \cup R_2$ are irreflexive

options.label: A
options.text: $R_1 \cap R_2$ is reflexive and $R_1 \cup R_2$ is irreflexive

options.label: B
options.text: $R_1 \cap R_2$ is irreflexive and $R_1 \cup R_2$ is reflexive

options.label: C
options.text: Both $R_1 \cap R_2$ and $R_1 \cup R_2$ are reflexive

options.label: D
options.text: Both $R_1 \cap R_2$ and $R_1 \cup R_2$ are irreflexive

questions.explanation: Let \( R_1 \) and \( R_2 \) be two reflexive relations on a set \( A \). By the definition of reflexivity:   \[ \forall a \in A,\ (a, a) \in R_1 \quad \text{and} \quad (a, a) \in R_2 \] Now consider: 1. Union: \[ R_1 \cup R_2 \]   Since \((a,a) \in R_1\) and \((a,a) \in R_2\), it follows that:   \[ \forall a \in A,\ (a,a) \in R_1 \cup R_2 \]   Therefore, \( R_1 \cup R_2 \) is reflexive. 2. Intersection: \[ R_1 \cap R_2 \]   Again, \((a,a)\) exists in both relations, hence:   \[ \forall a \in A,\ (a,a) \in R_1 \cap R_2 \]   Therefore, \( R_1 \cap R_2 \) is also reflexive. Hence, the correct answer is:   \[ \boxed{\text{A. Both } R_1 \cup R_2 \text{ and } R_1 \cap R_2 \text{ are reflexive}} \]

questions.questionText: Which of the following is false in the case of a spanning tree of a graph $\text{G}$? It is tree that spans $\text{G}$ It is a subgraph of the $\text{G}$ It includes every vertex of the $\text{G}$ It can be either cyclic or acyclic
questions.questionHtml:
Which of the following is false in the case of a spanning tree of a graph $\text{G}$?

  1. It is tree that spans $\text{G}$
  2. It is a subgraph of the $\text{G}$
  3. It includes every vertex of the $\text{G}$
  4. It can be either cyclic or acyclic

options.label: B
options.text: It is a subgraph of the $\text{G}$

options.label: C
options.text: It includes every vertex of the $\text{G}$

options.label: D
options.text: It can be either cyclic or acyclic

questions.explanation: Option A: It is a tree that spans G (TRUE) A spanning tree must satisfy the fundamental definition: it is a tree (connected and acyclic) that spans (includes all vertices of G). Option B: It is a subgraph of G (TRUE) By construction, a spanning tree uses a subset of the edges (E' \subseteq E) and the same set of vertices (V) from the original graph G. Option C: It includes every vertex of G (TRUE) The property of "spanning" dictates that the vertex set of the subgraph is identical to the vertex set of the parent graph . Option D: It can be either cyclic or acyclic (FALSE) By definition, a tree must be acyclic . A cyclic graph cannot be a tree. For a connected graph with n vertices, a spanning tree always has exactly n-1 edges and no cycles. Conclusion: Option D is the false statement. akash_kumar 9 answered Mar 6 akash_kumar 9 comment Share Follow 0 reply Please log in or register to add a comment. Voting & Accepting an answer helps improve the community Answer: D ←

questions.questionHtml:
Let $G=(V, E)$ be an undirected simple graph. A subset $M \subseteq E$ is a matching in $G$ if distinct edges in $M$ do not share a vertex. A matching is maximal if no strict superset of $M$ is a matching. How many maximal matchings does the following graph have?

  1. $1$
     
  2. $2$
     
  3. $3$
     
  4. $4$
questions.explanation: Let us first put lebels on the vertices :- Definition of matching :- Given a graph $G(V, E)$, a matching M in G is a set of pairwise set of non adjacent edges, that is no two edges shares common vertices. Definition of maximal matching :- A maximal matching is a matching of a graph $G$, that is not a subset of any other matching. So the maximal matching possible for the given question is :- 1. $\left\{e_1, e_3, e_5\right\}$ 2. $\left\{e_2, e_4\right\}$ 3. $\left\{e_1, e_4\right\}$ 4. $\left\{e_2, e_5\right\}$ Maximum matching is a matching that contain maximum number of pairwise non adjacent edges . Let $A=\{n \in[100,700] \cap \mathrm{N}: n$ is neither a multiple of $3$ nor a multiple of 4$\}$. Then the number of elements in $A$ is

  1. $300$
  2. $310$
  3. $290$

questions.explanation: The total number in this range are: $|S| = 700 - 100 + 1 = 601$ Let: $C_3$ = numbers in $S$ that are divisible by $3$ $C_4$ = numbers in $S$ that are divisible by $4$ We want to find the numbers that are not in $C_3 \cup C_4$ i.e : $|A| = |S| - |C_3 \cup C_4|$ $|C_3 \cup C_4| = |C_3| + |C_4| - |C_3 \cap C_4|$ $|C_3| = \left\lfloor \frac{700}{3} \right\rfloor - \left\lfloor \frac{99}{3} \right\rfloor = 233 - 33 = 200$ $|C_4| = \left\lfloor \frac{700}{4} \right\rfloor - \left\lfloor \frac{99}{4} \right\rfloor = 175 - 24 = 151$ $|C_3 \cap C_4| = \left\lfloor \frac{700}{12} \right\rfloor - \left\lfloor \frac{99}{12} \right\rfloor = 58 - 8 = 50$ $|C_3 \cup C_4|$ will be $200 + 151 - 50 = 301$ So: $|A| = 601 - 301 = \boxed{300}$ Abhishek-1011 answered Jul 22, 2025 Abhishek-1011 comment Share Follow See all 5 Comments 5 5 Comments reply Show 2 previous comments Amjad. commented Jul 22, 2025 reply Follow flag @Ryan 1  , tell me this is some joke  😂 0 0 reply Share Ryan 1 commented

questions.questionText: In order to select a debating team to represent a school, 7 students from class XII and 13 students from class XI were shortlisted and were undergoing trials. The coach had to select a team of 5 students, out of which at least two students should be from each class. One out of the 5 students was to be named as team leader, who was to be from class XII. Two teams with the same members but different leaders are considered to be two different teams. The number of different teams the coach can select is $2 \times\left(\binom{7}{2} \times\binom{ 13}{3}+\binom{7}{3} \times\binom{ 13}{2}\right)$ $\binom{7}{2} \times\binom{ 13}{3}+\binom{7}{3} \times\binom{ 13}{2}$ $2 \times\binom{ 7}{2} \times\binom{ 13}{3}+3 \times\binom{ 7}{3} \times\binom{ 13}{2}$ $3 \times\binom{ 7}{2} \times\binom{ 13}{3}+2 \times\binom{ 7}{3} \times\binom{ 13}{2}$
questions.questionHtml:
In order to select a debating team to represent a school, 7 students from class XII and 13 students from class XI were shortlisted and were undergoing trials. The coach had to select a team of 5 students, out of which at least two students should be from each class. One out of the 5 students was to be named as team leader, who was to be from class XII. Two teams with the same members but different leaders are considered to be two different teams. The number of different teams the coach can select is

  1. $2 \times\left(\binom{7}{2} \times\binom{ 13}{3}+\binom{7}{3} \times\binom{ 13}{2}\right)$
     
  2. $\binom{7}{2} \times\binom{ 13}{3}+\binom{7}{3} \times\binom{ 13}{2}$
     
  3. $2 \times\binom{ 7}{2} \times\binom{ 13}{3}+3 \times\binom{ 7}{3} \times\binom{ 13}{2}$
     
  4. $3 \times\binom{ 7}{2} \times\binom{ 13}{3}+2 \times\binom{ 7}{3} \times\binom{ 13}{2}$
questions.explanation: Choice C is correct, and choices A, B and D are wrong. Any choice of team either has exactly 2 students from class XII and exactly 3 students from class XI, OR it has exactly 3 students from class XII and exactly 2 students from class XI. The two terms in the sum in choice (c) correspond to these two cases. For each choice of $k \in\{2,3\}$ students from class XII, there are $k$ ways of choosing the leader. This is the leading term in each product in choice (c). Here is an alternate derivation: There are 7 ways of selecting a leader. For each leader selected, we can now pick either a single student from class XII or two students from class XII and the rest need to be from class XI. To form a team by selecting a single non-leader student from class XII, there are $7 \cdot\binom{6}{1} \cdot\binom{13}{3}$ ways. To form a team by selecting exactly two non-leader class XII students, there are exactly $7 \cdot\binom{6}{2} \cdot\binom{13}{2}$ ways. The answer is the sum of these.

questions.explanation: Let's take one particular assignment,say $A_{fixed}$. Given that two assignments are compatible if: 1.  There is at least one student who gets the same badge in both. 2.  There is at least one student who gets a different badge in both. An assignment $A_{new}$ is NOT compatible if it violates at least one of the two conditions. Violate Condition 1: This means NO student gets the same badge ,so EVERY student gets a different badge. For eg, if a student has a RED badge in $A_{fixed}$, he must have a BLUE badge in $A_{new}$, and vice-versa. So for  $A_{fixed}$, there is only one assignment where every student gets a different badge. Violate Condition 2: This means NO student gets a different badge so, EVERY student gets the same badge. questions.questionText: Suppose that we have a set of domino tiles . Each domino piece has a string at the top and a string at the bottom, for example: \[ \begin{array}{|c|} \hline abb \\ \hline bc \\ \hline \end{array} \] So a set \( S \) of dominos might look like: \[ S = \left\{ \begin{array}{|c|} \hline b \\ \hline ca \\ \hline \end{array}, \quad \begin{array}{|c|} \hline a \\ \hline ab \\ \hline \end{array}, \quad \begin{array}{|c|} \hline ca \\ \hline a \\ \hline \end{array}, \quad \begin{array}{|c|} \hline abc \\ \hline c \\ \hline \end{array} \right\} \] A match for \( S \) is an ordered list of one or more dominos from \( S \), such that if you read the symbols on the tops, this makes the same string as reading the symbols on the bottom. You can use the same domino more than once in a match, and you do not have to use all the elements of \( S \). questions.questionText: How many solutions are there to the equation $$x_1+x_2+x_3+x_4=21$$ where the order of the integers $x_1, x_2, x_3, x_4$ does not matter and $x_1, x_2, x_3, x_4 \geq 4$?
questions.questionHtml:
How many solutions are there to the equation
$$x_1+x_2+x_3+x_4=21$$

where the order of the integers $x_1, x_2, x_3, x_4$ does not matter and $x_1, x_2, x_3, x_4 \geq 4$?
questions.explanation: Replace each $x_i$ with $X_i=x_i-4$. We now need to count the number of solutions to $X_1+X_2+$ $X_3+X_4=5$ where the order of the integers $x_1, x_2, x_3, x_4$ does not matter and $x_1, x_2, x_3, x_4 \geq 0$. This is the problem of putting 5 indistinguishable objects into 4 indistinguishable boxes, so the answer is $p_1(5)+p_2(5)+p_3(5)+p_4(5)$ where $p_k(n)$ is the number of partitions of $n$ into $k$ positive integers. $$ \begin{array}{ll} p_1(5)=1 & (5) \\ p_2(5)=2 & (4+1,3+2) \\ p_3(5)=2 & (3+1+1,2+2+1) \\ p_4(5)=1 & (2+1+1+1) \end{array} $$ Therefore the answer is $p_1(5)+p_2(5)+p_3(5)+p_4(5)=1+2+2+1=6$. questions.questionText: Ox-words are sequences of letters $a$ and $b$ that are constructed according to the following rules: The sequence consisting of no letters is an oxword. If the sequence $W$ is an Ox-word, then the sequence that begins with $a$, followed by $W$ and ending in $b$, written $aWb$, is an Ox-word. If the sequences $U$ and $V$ are Ox-words, then the sequence $U$ followed by $V$, written $UV$, is an Ox-word. All Ox-words are constructed using these rules. The length of an Ox-word is the number of letters that occur in it.  For example, $aabb$ and $abab$ are Ox-words of length $4$. Which of the following statements is/are necessarily true for any Ox-word $W$? Every Ox word has an even length. The number of occurrences of $a$ in $W$ is necessarily equal to the number of occurrences of $b$ in $W$. In all prefixes of $W$, the number of occurrences of $a$ is greater than or equal to the number of occurrences of $b$. In all prefixes of $W$, the number of occurrences of $a$ is equal to the number of occurrences of $b$.
questions.questionHtml:
Ox-words are sequences of letters $a$ and $b$ that are constructed according to the following rules:

  • The sequence consisting of no letters is an oxword.
     
  • If the sequence $W$ is an Ox-word, then the sequence that begins with $a$, followed by $W$ and ending in $b$, written $aWb$, is an Ox-word.
     
  • If the sequences $U$ and $V$ are Ox-words, then the sequence $U$ followed by $V$, written $UV$, is an Ox-word.
     

All Ox-words are constructed using these rules. The length of an Ox-word is the number of letters that occur in it.

 For example, $aabb$ and $abab$ are Ox-words of length $4$.
 

Which of the following statements is/are necessarily true for any Ox-word $W$?
 

  1. Every Ox word has an even length.
     
  2. The number of occurrences of $a$ in $W$ is necessarily equal to the number of occurrences of $b$ in $W$.
     
  3. In all prefixes of $W$, the number of occurrences of $a$ is greater than or equal to the number of occurrences of $b$.
     
  4. In all prefixes of $W$, the number of occurrences of $a$ is equal to the number of occurrences of $b$.

options.label: A
options.text: Every Ox word has an even length.

options.label: B
options.text: The number of occurrences of $a$ in $W$ is necessarily equal to the number of occurrences of $b$ in $W$.

options.label: C
options.text: In all prefixes of $W$, the number of occurrences of $a$ is greater than or equal to the number of occurrences of $b$.

options.label: D
options.text: In all prefixes of $W$, the number of occurrences of $a$ is equal to the number of occurrences of $b$.

questions.excerpt: A sequence has $a_0=3$, and then for $n \geq 1$ the sequence satisfies $a_n=8\left(a_{n-1}\right)^4$The value of $a_{10}$ is$\frac{2^{\left(2^{20}\right)}}{3}$ $\frac{6^{...
questions.questionText: A sequence has $a_0=3$, and then for $n \geq 1$ the sequence satisfies $a_n=8\left(a_{n-1}\right)^4$ The value of $a_{10}$ is $\frac{2^{\left(2^{20}\right)}}{3}$ $\frac{6^{\left(2^{20}\right)}}{2}$ $\frac{6^{\left(2^{20}\right)}}{3}$ $\frac{3^{\left(2^{20}\right)}}{2}$
questions.questionHtml:
A sequence has $a_0=3$, and then for $n \geq 1$ the sequence satisfies $a_n=8\left(a_{n-1}\right)^4$

The value of $a_{10}$ is

  1. $\frac{2^{\left(2^{20}\right)}}{3}$
     
  2. $\frac{6^{\left(2^{20}\right)}}{2}$
     
  3. $\frac{6^{\left(2^{20}\right)}}{3}$
     
  4. $\frac{3^{\left(2^{20}\right)}}{2}$
questions.explanation: $a_1=8 \times(3)^4$ and $a_2=8\left(8 \times 3^4\right)^4=8 \times 8^4 \times\left(3^4\right)^4$ and $a_3=8 \times\left(8 \times 8^4 \times\left(3^4\right)^4\right)^4$. In a similar way, $$ a_n=8 \times 8^4 \times 8^{16} \times \cdots \times 8^{4^{n-1}} \times 3^{\left(4^n\right)} $$ The exponent on the 8 s is $1+4+16+\cdots+4^{n-1}=\frac{1}{3}\left(4^n-1\right)$. Then $8^{1 / 3}=2$. Also use $4^n=2^{2 n}$. $$ a_n=2^{2^{2 n}-1} 3^{\left(2^{2 n}\right)}=\frac{6^{2^{2 n}}}{2} $$ So for $n=10$ we get $\frac{6^{\left(2^{20}\right)}}{2}$. The answer is $\frac{6^{\left(2^{20}\right)}}{2}$. questions.questionText: If the expression $\left(x+1+\frac{1}{x}\right)^4$ is fully expanded term-by-term and like terms are collected together, there is one term which is independent of $x$. The value of this term is $10$ $19$ $51$ $14$
questions.questionHtml:
If the expression $\left(x+1+\frac{1}{x}\right)^4$ is fully expanded term-by-term and like terms are collected together,
there is one term which is independent of $x$.
The value of this term is

  1. $10$
     
  2. $19$
     
  3. $51$
     
  4. $14$
questions.explanation: The general term in $(a + b + c)^n$ is: $$ \frac{n!}{n_1! \, n_2! \, n_3!} \cdot a^{n_1} b^{n_2} c^{n_3} $$ where $n_1 + n_2 + n_3 = n$ and $n_i \ge 0$ So here the general term will be: $$ \frac{4!}{n_1! \, n_2! \, n_3!} \cdot x^{n_1} \cdot 1^{n_2} \cdot \left(\frac{1}{x}\right)^{n_3} = \frac{4!}{n_1! \, n_2! \, n_3!} \cdot x^{n_1 - n_3} $$ We want the term independent of x: So $n_1 = n_3$ Now just find valid $(n_1, n_2, n_3)$ satisfying the constraints that  $n_1 = n_3$ and $n_1 + n_2 + n_3 = 4$  $n_1 = 0$, $n_3 = 0$, then $n_2 = 4$   $n_1 = 1$, $n_3 = 1$, then $n_2 = 2$   $n_1 = 2$, $n_3 = 2$, then $n_2 = 0$   Now just calculate the coefficient for each valid triple For $(0, 4, 0)$: $$ \frac{4!}{0! \cdot 4! \cdot 0!} =  1 $$ For $(1, 2, 1)$: $$ \frac{4!}{1! \cdot 2! \cdot 1!} = 12 $$ For $(2, 0, 2)$: $$ \frac{4!}{2! \cdot 0! \cdot 2!} =  6 $$ Sum of all these constant-term coefficients: $1 + 12 + 6 = \boxed{19}$ Abhishek-1011 answered Jul 22,

questions.questionText: The coefficient of $x^{12}$ in $$ (1-2 x)^5\left(1+4 x^2\right)^5(1+2 x)^5 $$ is $-2^{13} \times 5$ $-2^{12} \times 5$ $2^{12} \times 5$ $2^{13} \times 5$
questions.questionHtml:
The coefficient of $x^{12}$ in
$$
(1-2 x)^5\left(1+4 x^2\right)^5(1+2 x)^5
$$
is

  1. $-2^{13} \times 5$
     
  2. $-2^{12} \times 5$
     
  3. $2^{12} \times 5$
     
  4. $2^{13} \times 5$
questions.explanation: Multiply out $(1 - 2x)(1 + 2x)$ first to get: $$ (1 - 2x)(1 + 2x) = 1 - 4x^2 $$ Then multiply that by $(1 + 4x^2)$ to get: $$ (1 - 4x^2)(1 + 4x^2) = 1 - 16x^4 $$ Now, expand $\left(1 - 16x^4\right)^5$ and look for the term with $x^{12}$ using binomial theorem: $$ \binom{5}{3} \cdot \left(-16x^4\right)^3 = 10 \cdot (-16)^3 \cdot x^{12} = -10 \times 2^{12} \cdot x^{12} $$ The answer is A. questions.questionHtml:
How many solutions are there to the equation $x_1+x_2+x_3+x_4=20$ where $x_1, x_2, x_3, x_4$ are nonnegative integers where
$$
2 \leq x_1 \leq 5 ?
$$
questions.explanation: Using lower bound $x_1 \ge 2$ Then number of non-negative integer solutions will be: $\binom{18 + 4 - 1}{4 - 1} = \binom{21}{3} = \frac{21 \cdot 20 \cdot 19}{6} = 1330$ Now subtract cases where $x_1 > 5$ i.e., $x_1 \ge 6$ So, mumber of non-negative integer solutions where condition is violated : $\binom{14 + 4 - 1}{4 - 1} = \binom{17}{3} = \frac{17 \cdot 16 \cdot 15}{6} = 680$ So, total violating solutions where $x_1 \ge 6$ are $680$ Valid solutions will be $1330 - 680 = \boxed{650}$ Abhishek-1011 answered Jul 22, 2025 Abhishek-1011 comment Share Follow 0 reply Please log in or register to add a comment. What is the coefficient of $x^{5}$ is $\mathrm{G}(x)?$
questions.questionHtml:
Define the generating functions $\text{B}(x)=\displaystyle{} \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} 2^{n} x^{n}$ and $F(x)=\displaystyle{} \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} f_{n} x^{n}$ where $f_{n}$ is the Fibonacci sequence determined by the recurrence relation
$$
\begin{aligned}
f_{0} &=0 \quad \text { and } \quad f_{1}=1 \\
f_{n} &=f_{n-1}+f_{n-2} & \text { for } n \geq 2\\
\end{aligned}
$$
Let $\text{G}(x)=\text{B}(x) \times \text{F}(x)$.

What is the coefficient of $x^{5}$ is $\mathrm{G}(x)?$
questions.explanation: $$ \begin{aligned} &\text{G}(x)=\text{B}(x) \times \text{F}(x) \\ &=\left(2^{0} x^{0}+2^{1} x^{1}+2^{2} x^{2}+2^{3} x^{3}+2^{4} x^{4}+2^{5} x^{5}+2 ^{6} x^{6}+\ldots\right) \times \\ &\left(1 x^{1}+1 x^{2}+2 x^{3}+3 x^{4}+5 x^{5}+8 x^{6}+\ldots\right) \end{aligned} $$ So, Coefficient of $x^{5}$ will be: $5+6+8+8+16=43$. questions.questionHtml:

How many staircase walks are there from $\text{A}$ to $\text{B}$ which start by going to the right two times?
questions.explanation: We can only reach the grid point $(2, 0)$ by making two moves to the right in the beginning. Therefore, the total number of staircase walks on this grid that start by moving right twice is exactly the same as the number of staircase walks from $(2, 0)$ to $\text{B}$, namely ${}^{12}\text{C}_{3}$. In other words, we need to choose $3$ up moves out of a total of $12$ remaining moves to make it to $\text{B}$ (the rest are right moves). questions.explanation: The recurrence relation for $\text{T}_{n}$ will be: $$ \text{T}_{n} = 2 \text{T}_{n-1} + 2 \text{T}_{n-3} $$ Since the initial conditions are already given: $$ \text{T}_{4} = 28; \quad \text{T}_{5} = 66; \quad \text{T}_{6} = 156; \quad \text{T}_{7} = 368. $$ Watch the complete Recurrence Relations in Discrete Mathematics playlist to understand the concept: Watch Complete Playlist GO Classes answered Jul 20, 2025 • edited Jul 20, 2025 by GO Classes GO Classes comment Share Follow 0 reply Please log in or register to add a comment. questions.questionHtml:
In the expansion of $\left(x^2+x y+y^2\right)^n$, where $n$ is a positive whole number, the coefficient of $x^3 y^{2 n-3}$ is

  1. $\binom{n}{3}$
     
  2. $\binom{n}{3} \times\binom{ n}{2}$
     
  3. $\binom{n}{3}+2 \times\binom{ n}{2}$
     
  4. $2 \times\binom{ n}{2}$
questions.explanation: B The first few terms of the binomial expansion of $\left(\left(x^2+x y\right)+y^2\right)^n$ are $$ \binom{n}{0} y^{2 n}+\binom{n}{1}\left(x^2+x y\right) y^{2 n-2}+\binom{n}{2}\left(x^2+x y\right)^2 y^{2 n-4}+\binom{n}{3}\left(x^2+x y\right)^3 y^{2 n-6}+\ldots $$ The first two terms don't contain any $x^3 y^{2 n-3}$ terms, and any terms after these four must have a factor of $x^4$, so they don't contribute either. We need to think about the expansion of $\left(x^2+x y\right)^2$ which includes $2 x^2 x y$, and the expansion of $\left(x^2+x y\right)^3$ which includes $(x y)^3$. So the coefficient is $2 \times\binom{ n}{2}+\binom{n}{3}$. questions.questionText: $10$ oranges are to be placed in $5$ distinct boxes labeled $\mathrm{U}, \mathrm{V}, \mathrm{W}, \mathrm{X}, \mathrm{Y}$. A box may contain any number of oranges including no oranges or all the oranges. What is the number of ways to distribute the oranges so that exactly two of the boxes contain exactly two oranges each?
questions.questionHtml: $10$ oranges are to be placed in $5$ distinct boxes labeled $\mathrm{U}, \mathrm{V}, \mathrm{W}, \mathrm{X}, \mathrm{Y}$. A box may contain any number of oranges including no oranges or all the oranges. What is the number of ways to distribute the oranges so that exactly two of the boxes contain exactly two oranges each?
questions.explanation: Solution. From the five distinct boxes, there are 10 ways to pick the two boxes that will have 2 oranges each. We need to distribute the remaining 6 oranges in the remaining three boxes such that none of the three boxes gets exactly 2 oranges. The possible distributions are $6+0+0$ (which can be done in 3 ways) or $5+1+0$ ( 6 ways) or $4+1+1$ ( 3 ways) or $3+3+0$ ( 3 ways). Thus the required answer is $10 \times(3+6+3+3)=150$. GO Classes answered Jul 20, 2025 GO Classes comment Share Follow 0 reply Please log in or register to add a comment. 1 1 vote From 5 boxes 2 have exactly 2 oranges each.  Number of ways to choose 2 boxes among 5 boxes = 5C2 = 10. After we have filled 2 boxes with 4 oranges, we have 3 boxes and 6 oranges left. Note: Once we have chosen 2 boxes to have 2 oranges each we cannot put exactly 2 oranges in the remaining boxes. This will violate the condition that only 2 boxes have exactly 2 oranges. Invalid possibilities of orange share in the 3 boxes: 4 + 2 + 0&n

questions.questionHtml:
Let $N=\{1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8,9\}$ and $L=\{a, b, c\}$.
Suppose we arrange $12$ elements of $\mathrm{L} U \mathrm{~N}$ in a line such that no two of the three letters occur consecutively. If the order of the letters among themselves does not matter, find the number of such arrangements.
questions.explanation: Imagine that the numbers are placed with a gap between two consecutive numbers. Moreover there is a gap before $1$ and one after $9$. So there are $10$ gaps, where letters can be placed. In order to find the number of such arrangement first choose $3$ gaps from $10$ and then permute the $9$ numbers. The final answer is $\binom{10}{3} \cdot 9!$. GO Classes answered Jul 20, 2025 GO Classes comment Share Follow 0 reply Please log in or register to add a comment. If the entire seating arrangement is to be chosen at random, what is the probability that all of the men will be seated next to each other in $6$ consecutive positions? $\frac{1}{\binom{15}{6}}$ $\frac{6!}{\binom{15}{6}}$ $\frac{10!}{15!}$ $\frac{6!10!}{15!}$
questions.questionHtml:
At a banquet, $9$ women and $6$ men are to be seated in a row of $15$ chairs. If the entire seating arrangement is to be chosen at random, what is the probability that all of the men will be seated next to each other in $6$ consecutive positions?

  1. $\frac{1}{\binom{15}{6}}$
     
  2. $\frac{6!}{\binom{15}{6}}$
     
  3. $\frac{10!}{15!}$
     
  4. $\frac{6!10!}{15!}$
questions.explanation: The total number of ways to sit for all men and women = (9+6)! = 15! Case: When all men are seated together consecutively Let us consider all 6 men as 1 unit, then we have 1 unit of men and 9 women = 10 units Total number of ways to arrange 10 units = 10! However, the men inside the unit can arrange among themselves in 6! ways Therefore the number of ways all men are seated together = 10! x 6! Probability = (10! x 6!)/15! rextrinsic answered Jul 21, 2025 rextrinsic comment Share Follow 0 reply Please log in or register to add a comment. questions.questionHtml: What is the minimum number of elements that must be selected from the set $\{1,2,3, \ldots, 50\}$ to ensure that at least two of them are consecutive?
questions.explanation: We are selecting numbers from the set $\{1,2,3, \ldots, 50\}$ and want to ensure that at least two of them are consecutive. To avoid choosing any two consecutive numbers, we can pick numbers like this: $$ 1,3,5,7, \ldots, 49 $$ This way, there's always a gap between any two selected numbers. Using this method, we can pick at most $25$ numbers without any two being consecutive. But the moment we pick $26$ numbers, at least one pair will be forced to be consecutive.

questions.questionText: How many arrangements of the digits $0,1, \ldots, 9$ are there that do not end with a $1$ and do not begin with a $9$ ?
questions.questionHtml: How many arrangements of the digits $0,1, \ldots, 9$ are there that do not end with a $1$ and do not begin with a $9$ ?
questions.explanation: Total number of permutations of the $10$ digits ( $0$ to $9$ ) is: $$ 10!=3628800 $$ Now subtract the invalid cases using inclusion-exclusion: Number of permutations that end with 1: Fix 1 at the last position, arrange remaining $9$ digits $\rightarrow$ $$ 9!=362880 $$ Number of permutations that start with $9$: Fix 9 at the first position, arrange remaining $9$ digits $\rightarrow$ $$ 9!=362880 $$ Number of permutations that start with 9 and end with 1 : Fix 9 at the start and 1 at the end, arrange remaining 8 digits $\rightarrow$ $$ 8!=40320 $$ Applying inclusion-exclusion: $$ \begin{gathered} \text { Valid permutations }=10!-(\text { End with } 1+\text { Start with } 9-\text { Both }) \\ =3628800-(362880+362880-40320)=3628800-685440=2943360 \end{gathered} $$ GO Classes answered Jul 14, 2025 • reshown Jul 17, 2025 by GO Classes Support GO Classes comment Share Follow 0 reply Please log in or register to add a comment. 0 0 votes 10!-9!-9!+8!  Inclusion exclusion principle A

questions.questionHtml:
Let $A=\{1,2,3, \ldots, 18\}$. Four mutually distinct elements $x_1, x_2, x_3, x_4 \in A$ are selected.
Determine the minimum positive integer $y$ such that no matter which 4 distinct elements are chosen from $A$, there will always exist two elements $x_i, x_j$ (with $i \neq j$ ) satisfying:

$$
\left|x_i-x_j\right| \leq y
$$
questions.explanation: We check values of $y$ from 1 to 4 : For $y=1:\{1,3,5,7\} \rightarrow$ all differences $\geq 2$ For $y=2:\{1,4,7,10\} \rightarrow$ all differences $\geq 3$ For $y=3:\{1,5,9,13\} \rightarrow$ all differences $\geq 4$ For $y=4:\{1,6,11,16\} \rightarrow$ all differences $\geq 5$ So, for $y=1,2,3,4$, we can pick 4 elements with all pairwise differences $>y$. Hence, these are not valid. Now try $y=5$ : To get all differences $>5$, we need gaps of at least 6 . Try: $$ \{1,7,13,19\} \rightarrow \text { But } 19 \text { not in set }\{1,2, \ldots, 18\} $$ So, it's impossible to pick 4 such elements. Therefore, minimum valid $y=5$. questions.explanation: A graph is said to be a bipartite graph, when vertices of that graph can be divided into two independent sets such that every edge in the graph is either start from the first set and ended in the second set connected to the first set, in other words, we can say that no edge can found in the same set. Bipartite graphs are precisely the class of graphs that are $2$ -colorable. Checking of a bipartite graph is possible by using the vertex coloring. When a vertex is in the same set, it has the same color, for another set, the color will change. For the given option we can see only option $2$) is $2$-colorable graph. Moreover, a bipartite graph has no odd length cycle which is not present in option $2$) Hence Option $2$) is correct answer

questions.questionText: An induced subgraph of an undirected graph $G = (V,E)$ is a graph formed from a non-empty subset $S$ of the vertices $V$ and all of the edges in $E$ connecting pairs of vertices in $S$. The $degeneracy$ of an undirected graph $G = (V,E)$ is the $minimum$ integer $k$ such that every induced subgraph of the graph has a vertex with degree at most $k$. Prove or disprove the following claims: The degeneracy of a graph is equal to the maximum degree of any vertex in the graph. A tree (connected acyclic graph) on $n > 1$ vertices has degeneracy $1$. If $G$ has degeneracy $k$, then $G$ - $v$ has degeneracy at most $k$, for every $v \in V$. $G$ has degeneracy $k$ if and only if its vertices can be ordered as $v_1,v_2,...,v_n$ such that $v_i$ has degree at most $k$ in $G[v_i,...,v_n]$, the induced subgraph on $[v_i,...,v_n]$.
questions.questionHtml:
An induced subgraph of an undirected graph $G = (V,E)$ is a graph formed from a non-empty subset $S$ of the vertices $V$ and all of the edges in $E$ connecting pairs of vertices in $S$. The $degeneracy$ of an undirected graph $G = (V,E)$ is the $minimum$ integer $k$ such that every induced subgraph of the graph has a vertex with degree at most $k$. Prove or disprove the following claims:

  1. The degeneracy of a graph is equal to the maximum degree of any vertex in the graph.
  2. A tree (connected acyclic graph) on $n > 1$ vertices has degeneracy $1$.
  3. If $G$ has degeneracy $k$, then $G$ - $v$ has degeneracy at most $k$, for every $v \in V$.
  4. $G$ has degeneracy $k$ if and only if its vertices can be ordered as $v_1,v_2,...,v_n$ such that $v_i$ has degree at most $k$ in $G[v_i,...,v_n]$, the induced subgraph on $[v_i,...,v_n]$.

options.label: A
options.text: The degeneracy of a graph is equal to the maximum degree of any vertex in the graph.

options.label: B
options.text: A tree (connected acyclic graph) on $n > 1$ vertices has degeneracy $1$.

options.label: C
options.text: If $G$ has degeneracy $k$, then $G$ - $v$ has degeneracy at most $k$, for every $v \in V$.

questions.explanation: ​ $ \textit{(a): The degeneracy of a graph is equal to the maximum degree of any vertex in the graph.} $ Consider the star graph $ K_{1,6} $ the maximum degree here is $ \Delta = 6 $ Let’s consider all induced subgraphs: $ \textbf{Case 1:} $ Any subgraph with only leaves (no $ c $)   No edges, so degrees are 0 $ \le k $ for any $ k \ge 0 $. $ \textbf{Case 2:} $ Subgraph with $ c $ and some leaves   ​Each leaf still has degree 1, $ c $ has degree equal to number of included leaves (at most 6), But there is always at least one leaf of degree 1 $ \le 1 $. So every induced subgraph has a vertex of degree $ \le 1 $. Therefore, degeneracy is: \[ \text{Degeneracy} = 1 \ne \Delta \] So the statement is false. ​ $ \textit{(b): A tree on $n > 1$ vertices has degeneracy 1.} $ A tree is connected and acyclic. Any induced subgraph of a tree is a forest (collection of trees), and each component has at least one leaf.            from the above figures

questions.questionText: Let $G = (V,E)$ be an undirected connected graph with a cost, $c_e \geq 0$ on each edge e. The costs on the edges may not all be different. A minimum-cost spanning tree of $G$ is a tree $T$ that spans $G$ and also minimizes the sum of the costs of the edges in $T$. Since the costs are not all distinct, there can, in general, be many distinct minimum-cost spanning trees. Suppose we are given a spanning tree $T \subseteq E$ with the guarantee that for every edge $e \in T$, the edge $e$ belongs to some minimum-cost spanning tree in $G$. Can we conclude that $T$ itself must be a minimum-cost spanning tree in $G?$ Give a proof or counterexample to the claim.
questions.questionHtml: Let $G = (V,E)$ be an undirected connected graph with a cost, $c_e \geq 0$ on each edge e. The costs on the edges may not all be different. A minimum-cost spanning tree of $G$ is a tree $T$ that spans $G$ and also minimizes the sum of the costs of the edges in $T$. Since the costs are not all distinct, there can, in general, be many distinct minimum-cost spanning trees. Suppose we are given a spanning tree $T \subseteq E$ with the guarantee that for every edge $e \in T$, the edge $e$ belongs to some minimum-cost spanning tree in $G$. Can we conclude that $T$ itself must be a minimum-cost spanning tree in $G?$ Give a proof or counterexample to the claim.
questions.explanation: Consider the undirected connected graph \( G = (V, E) \) with vertices \( V = \{A, B, C\} \) \[ \textbf{The MSTs of \( G \) are:} \] - \( \text{MST}_1 = \{(A, B), (A, C)\} \) with total cost \( 1 + 2 = 3 \), -\( \text{MST}_2 = \{(A, B), (B, C)\} \) with total cost \( 1 + 2 = 3 \). Now,take this spanning tree \( T = \{(A, C), (B, C)\} \)    Total cost \( 2 + 2 = 4 \), which is greater than the MST cost of 3. Therefore, \( T \) is not an MST. However, every edge in \( T \) belongs to some MST: - Edge \( (A, C) \) belongs to \( \text{MST}_1 \), - Edge \( (B, C) \) belongs to \( \text{MST}_2 \). So, although \( T \) satisfies the condition that every edge belongs to some MST, \( T \) is not an MST. questions.questionHtml:
Let $S = \sum_{n\geq1} \dfrac{1}{n^2}$ and $A = \sum_{n\geq1}(-1)^{n+1}\dfrac{1}{n^2}$. Then which of the following statements is true?

  1. $S$ converges but $A$ does not converge.
  2. $A$ converges but $S$ does not converge.
  3. Both $S$ and $A$ diverge.
  4. Both $S$ and $A$ converge and $S=2A$.
questions.explanation: The series $S = \sum_{n \geq 1} \frac{1}{n^2}$ is a $p$-series with $p = 2 > 1$. By the $p$-series test, $S$ converges. The series $A = \sum_{n \geq 1} (-1)^{n+1} \frac{1}{n^2}$ is an alternating series. The absolute value of the terms is $|(-1)^{n+1} \frac{1}{n^2}| = \frac{1}{n^2}$, which is monotonically decreasing and approaches $0$ as $n \to \infty$. By the alternating series test, $A$ converges. Reference: https://www.csusm.edu/mathlab/documents/seriesconvergediverge.pdf $A$ can be written as: \[ A = \frac{1}{1^2} - \frac{1}{2^2} + \frac{1}{3^2} - \frac{1}{4^2} + \frac{1}{5^2} - \cdots \] \[  = \left( \frac{1}{1^2} + \frac{1}{3^2} + \frac{1}{5^2} + \cdots \right) - \left( \frac{1}{2^2} + \frac{1}{4^2} + \frac{1}{6^2} + \cdots \right) \] The sum of the $\textbf{odd-indexed terms}$ is: \[ \sum_{k=1}^\infty \frac{1}{(2k - 1)^2} \] The sum of the $\textbf{even-indexed terms}$ is: \[ \sum_{k=1}^\infty \frac{1}{(2k)^2} = \sum_{k=1}^\infty \frac{1}{4k^2} = \frac{1}{4} \sum_{k=1}

questions.explanation: (i) \( T \) has no cycles and \( n - 1 \) edges. A tree is an acyclic connected graph, and a tree with \( n \) vertices has exactly \( n - 1 \) edges. \(\Rightarrow\) True. (ii) There are edges in \( T \) that are not cut edges. In a tree, every edge is a cut-edge. \(\Rightarrow\) False. (iii) There are vertices in \( T \) that are connected by more than one path. In a tree, there is a unique path between any two vertices.   So more than one path between any two vertices is not possible. \(\Rightarrow\) False. (iv) \( T \) contains no cycle but addition of any new edge creates exactly one cycle. Since a tree already has a unique path between any two vertices, adding a new edge creates a single cycle. \(\Rightarrow\) True. \[ \boxed{\text{Option C is correct.}} \] Source

questions.explanation: Let \( m = \lceil \sqrt[3]{x} \rceil \), we need \( x^m \) to be a perfect cube. \( m=1 \implies x=1 \). \( m=2 \implies x \in [2,8] \). Only 8 will work. \( m=3 \implies x \in [9,27] \). All will work. \( m=4 \implies x \in [28,64] \). Only 64 will work. \( m=5 \implies x \in [65,125] \). No one works. \[ \text{Total} = 1+1+19+1 = 22 \] Abhishek-1011 answered Jul 2, 2025 • edited Sep 11, 2025 by Abhishek-1011 1 flag: ✌ Edit necessary (jayy_patel “incorrect answer”)

Let $F_n$ denote the $n^{th}$ fibonacci number, where $F_0 := 0$, $F_1 := 1$ and $F_{n+1} := F_n + F_{n-1}$. Which of the following statements is true about $a_n?$ There exists an $n$ such that $a_n < \frac{F_n}{F_{n+1}}$ There exists an $n$ such that $a_n > \frac{F_n}{F_{n+1}}$ For all $n, a_n = \frac{F_{n+1}}{F_n}$ For all $n, a_n = \frac{F_n}{F_{n+1}}$
questions.questionHtml:
Consider the rational number $a_n$ defined recursively as $a_n$ = $\dfrac{1}{1 + a_{n-1}}$, where $a_0 := 0$. Let $F_n$ denote the $n^{th}$ fibonacci number, where $F_0 := 0$, $F_1 := 1$ and $F_{n+1} := F_n + F_{n-1}$. Which of the following statements is true about $a_n?$

  1. There exists an $n$ such that $a_n < \frac{F_n}{F_{n+1}}$
  2. There exists an $n$ such that $a_n > \frac{F_n}{F_{n+1}}$
  3. For all $n, a_n = \frac{F_{n+1}}{F_n}$
  4. For all $n, a_n = \frac{F_n}{F_{n+1}}$
questions.explanation: The sequence \( a_n \) is defined recursively as \[ a_n = \frac{1}{1 + a_{n-1}} \text{ for } n \geq 1 \quad,\quad a_0 = 0 \] Fibonacci sequence is given by \[ F_0 = 0, \quad F_1 = 1, \quad F_{n+1} = F_n + F_{n-1} \text{ for } n \geq 1 \] The first few terms of \( a_n \) are: \( a_0 = 0 \) \( a_1 = \frac{1}{1 + a_0} = \frac{1}{1 + 0} = 1 \) \( a_2 = \frac{1}{1 + a_1} = \frac{1}{1 + 1} = \frac{1}{2} \) \( a_3 = \frac{1}{1 + a_2} = \frac{1}{1 + \frac{1}{2}} = \frac{2}{3} \) The Fibonacci sequence is: \( 0, 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, 21, \ldots \) To prove that \( a_n = \frac{F_n}{F_{n+1}} \) for all \( n \geq 0 \), we can use induction. $\textit{Base case}$: For \( n = 0 \): \( a_0 = 0 \), \( \frac{F_0}{F_1} = \frac{0}{1} = 0 \), so true.   3. 0

questions.explanation: A 3-regular graph has each of its 5 vertices with degree 3, so the total degree is $5 \times 3 = 15$. But by the handshaking lemma, the sum of degrees in any graph must be even Here, it's $15$ , which is not possible. So, no 3-regular induced subgraph on 5 vertices can exist in $\textit{any graph}$. Thus,it is $\boxed{0}$. questions.questionHtml:
Let the sequence $\left\{a_n\right\}$ be defined by:

$$
a_0=1, \quad a_1=6, \quad \text { and } \quad a_{n+1}=6 a_n-9 a_{n-1} \text { for } n \geq 1 .
$$


Which of the following is the closed-form expression for $a_n$ ?

  1. $a_n=3^n$
     
  2. $a_n=(n+1) \cdot 3^n$
     
  3. $a_n=2^n+3^n$

questions.explanation: The recurrence is: $$ a_{n+1}=6 a_n-9 a_{n-1} $$ This is a linear recurrence with constant coefficients. The characteristic equation is: $$ r^2-6 r+9=0 \Rightarrow(r-3)^2=0 $$ So the general solution is: $$ a_n=(A+B n) \cdot 3^n $$ Use initial values: $a_0=(A+0) \cdot 1=A=1$ $a_1=(A+B) \cdot 3=6 \Rightarrow(1+B) \cdot 3=6 \Rightarrow B=1$ So: $$ a_n=(1+n) \cdot 3^n $$ GO Classes answered Jun 30, 2025 • reshown Jul 2, 2025 by GO Classes Support GO Classes comment Share Follow 0 reply Please log in or register to add a comment. 0 0 votes Option B should be correct For n = 0,      A) a(0) = 3^0 =1                      B) a(0) = (0 + 1)3^0 = 1                      C) a(0) = 2^0 + 3^0 = 1 + 1 = 2; So C is FALSE                        D) a(0) = (3*0+1)^0 = (1)^0  = 1 For n = 1,  &nbsp

Compute the number of all possible rearrangements of the following sequence of letters

$$
A A A B B B C C C
$$

such that no three identical consecutive letters exist (that is no strings of the form $AAA$ or $BBB$ or $CCC$ exist in the rearrangment).
questions.explanation: Total arrangements: 9!/3!3!3! = 1680 We need to subtract the cases where there is “AAA” or “BBB” or “CCC”. Let: A1​: arrangements with “AAA” A2​: arrangements with “BBB” A3​: arrangements with “CCC” We need: N = Total − ∣A1∪A2∪A3∣ Using: ∣A1∪A2∪A3∣=∣A1∣+∣A2∣+∣A3∣−∣A1∩A2∣−∣A1∩A3∣−∣A2∩A3∣+∣A1∩A2∩A3∣ Compute ∣A1∣: Treat “AAA” as a block → reduces count: “AAA” (1 block) BBB (3) CCC (3) We now have: 1 “AAA” block B, B, B C, C, C Total items: 1 + 3 + 3 = 7 items with: B: 3 C: 3 AAA: 1 Arrangements: 7!/3!3! = 140 By symmetry: ∣A1∣=∣A2∣=∣A3∣=140 Compute ∣A1∩A2∣: Now “AAA” and “BBB” are blocks: 1 “AAA” 1 “BBB” C, C, C Total items: 1 + 1 + 3 = 5 items with: C: 3 AAA: 1 BBB: 1 Arrangements: 5!/3!=20 Similarly: ∣A1∩A2∣=∣A1∩A3∣=∣A2∩A3∣=20 Compute ∣A1∩A2∩A3∣: All “AAA”, “BBB”, “CCC” as blocks: 1 “AAA” 1 “BBB” 1 “CCC” Total items = 3, all distinct. Arrangements: 3!=6 ∣A1∪A2∪A3∣=140+140+140−20−20−20+6=366 Final answer: N=1680−366= 1314 Ujjwal_Singh answered Jul 12, 2025 Ujjwal_Singh comment

Q1. Let $A$ be a subset of $n+1$ numbers chosen from the set $\{1,2,3, \ldots, 2 n\}$, where $n$ is a natural number. Which of the following must be true?

  1. All elements in $A$ are even
     
  2. No two elements in $A$ are consecutive
     
  3. At least two elements in $A$ are consecutive
     
  4. All elements in $A$ are odd

options.label: B
options.text: No two elements in $A$ are consecutive

options.label: C
options.text: At least two elements in $A$ are consecutive

questions.explanation: We are given a set: $$ \{1,2,3, \ldots, 2 n\} $$ and told to select $n+1$ elements from this set. Now, divide this set into $n$ pigeonholes , each pigeonhole being a pair of non-consecutive numbers: $$ \{1,2\},\{3,4\}, \ldots,\{2 n-1,2 n\} $$ That's a total of $n$ such pairs (each pair holds at most one non-consecutive number). Since we're choosing $n+1$ numbers (i.e., more than $n$ pigeonholes), by the Pigeonhole Principle , at least one pigeonhole must contain two elements , i.e., at least two chosen numbers will land in the same pair $\{i, i+1\}$, meaning they are consecutive. The number of sequences of ten terms, whose terms are either 0 or 1 or 2 , that contain exactly five 1 s and exactly three 2 s , is equal to:

  1. $360$
     
  2. $2520$
     
  3. $1820$

questions.explanation: To find the number of sequences of ten terms, each being either 0,1 , or 2 , containing exactly five 1 s and exactly three 2 s , follow these steps: Determine the Remaining Terms : Since there are 5 ones and 3 twos, you will need 2 zeros to fill the sequence (because $5+3+2=10$ ). Calculate the Number of Arrangements: You have a total of 10 positions to fill with these numbers ( 5 ones, 3 twos, 2 zeros). The formula for calculating permutations of a multiset is: $$ \frac{10!}{3!\times 3!\times 2!} $$ Where: $10!$ is the factorial of the total number of terms. 5 ! is the factorial for the number of 1 s . 3 ! is the factorial for the number of 2 s . $2!$ is the factorial for the number of 0 s . Result: Simplifying the calculation gives: $$ \frac{10!}{3!\times 3!\times 2!}=2520 $$ Thus, there are 2520 possible sequences with the given conditions. questions.questionHtml:
Let $G$ be a finite group and consider the following statements, which of the following statement are true?

  1. If $G$ has even order, then it contains an element $a \neq e$ such that $a^2=e$.
     
  2. For any finite group $G$, there exists a positive integer $N$ such that $a^N=e$ for all $a \in G$.
